parts.problem_md:
**Bioethanol as a renewable fuel**

Bioethanol is ethanol (CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH) produced by the fermentation of sugars derived from plant crops. In the UK, 'E5' petrol contains up to 5% bioethanol by volume, blended with conventional petrol (which is a mixture of liquid alkanes).

The displayed formula of glucose (the sugar commonly used to produce bioethanol) is shown below.

![Chemical structure of D-glucose, showing a linear six-carbon chain with hydroxyl groups and an aldehyde group at the top.](assets/007-chemical-structure-of-d-glucose-showing-a-linear.jpg)

Identify the **two** functional groups present in the glucose molecule.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The two functional groups present in the glucose molecule:
> 
> - Hydroxyl group / –OH (group) / alcohol **[1 mark]**
> - Aldehyde group / –CHO
> **OR**
> Carbonyl at end of chain **[1 mark]**
> 
> Hydroxide / OH<sup>-</sup> is not accepted for the first mark.
> 
> "Carbonyl" alone and "ketone" are not accepted for the second mark.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The four common functional groups containing a C=O are:
> 
> - Aldehyde (–CHO, at a terminal carbon)
> - Ketone (C=O within the chain)
> - Carboxylic acid (–COOH)
> - Ester (–COO–)
> 
> Be specific as writing just "carbonyl" is too vague and will not score. Glucose has a terminal C=O (aldehyde) and several –OH groups (hydroxyls).
> 
> Do not confuse "hydroxide" (the OH<sup>-</sup> ion) with "hydroxyl" (the –OH group attached to a carbon).

parts.problem_md:
During fermentation, glucose is converted to ethanol and carbon dioxide by the action of enzymes in yeast.

Write the balanced chemical equation for the fermentation of glucose, and state the conditions required for the reaction.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The equation for the fermentation of glucose is:
> 
> - C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>6</sub>→2CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH+2CO<sub>2</sub>
> **OR**
> C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>6</sub> → 2C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH + 2CO<sub>2</sub> **[1 mark]**
> 
> The required conditions are:
> 
> - Yeast / zymase / enzyme from yeast **[1 mark]**
> - Anaerobic / no oxygen / absence of oxygen
> **AND **
> An appropriate warm temperature (30 °C−40 °C) **[1 mark]**
> 
> Unbalanced equations and equations including H<sub>2</sub>O as a product are not accepted.

> **[exam-tip]**
> A common slip is to include water as a product. Fermentation produces only ethanol and CO<sub>2</sub>. Check your equation: 1 mol glucose gives 2 mol ethanol + 2 mol CO<sub>2</sub>.
> 
> Always state "anaerobic" (or "no oxygen") in your conditions. If oxygen were present, the ethanol would be oxidised to ethanoic acid instead.

parts.problem_md:
E5 petrol is a blend of bioethanol with liquid alkanes. Hexane (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>14</sub>) is a typical component of petrol.

The boiling points are: ethanol = 78 °C; hexane = 69 °C.

Compare and explain the intermolecular forces present in ethanol and hexane, and explain why ethanol has the higher boiling point despite having a lower molecular mass.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Comparison of intermolecular forces in ethanol and hexane:
> 
> - Ethanol has London dispersion forces (LDF) 
> **AND **
> Hydrogen bonding **[1 mark]**
> - Hexane has London dispersion forces (LDF) only **[1 mark]**
> - Hydrogen bonds are stronger than London forces **[1 mark]**
> - Therefore more energy is required to break the intermolecular forces in ethanol, resulting in a higher boiling point for ethanol **[1 mark]**
> 
> Just "dispersion forces" and  van der Waals' forces are accepted instead of London dispersion forces (LDF)
> 
> "As *M*<sub>r</sub> increases, boiling point increases" without reference to electrons or intermolecular force is not accepted.

> **[exam-tip]**
> This is a classic trap: smaller molecular mass does not always mean a lower boiling point. That only holds when the intermolecular forces are the same type. When one molecule can hydrogen bond and the other cannot, hydrogen bonding usually dominates, even if the other molecule has stronger London dispersion forces.
> 
> Structure your answer around four things:
> 
> 1. What IMFs are present in each molecule
> 2. Their relative strengths
> 3. Which type is dominant
> 4. The combined energy and boiling-point conclusion

parts.problem_md:
i) Use your equation from part (b) to calculate the percentage atom economy for the production of ethanol by the fermentation of glucose.

[*M*<sub>r</sub> values: C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>6</sub> = 180.0; CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH = 46.0; CO<sub>2</sub> = 44.0]

Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

[3]

ii) State why fermentation is considered a more sustainable method of producing ethanol than the alternative route of hydration of ethene from crude oil, even though its atom economy is lower.

[2]
parts.solution_md:
i) To calculate the atom economy:

- Write the atom economy formula:

percentage atom economy = $\frac{M_{r}\text{of desired product}}{\text{sum of}M_{r}\text{of all products}}$ x 100

- Using the fermentation equation (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>6</sub> → 2CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH + 2CO<sub>2</sub>), calculate the molar mass of the desired product:

2 × 46.0 = 92.0

**[1 mark]**

- Substitute values with stoichiometric coefficients (coefficient of 2 on ethanol and CO<sub>2</sub>):

percentage atom economy = `\frac{2 \times 46 . 0}{\left(\right. 2 \times 46 . 0 \left.\right) + \left(\right. 2 \times 44 . 0 \left.\right)}` x 100

percentage atom economy = $\frac{92.0}{180.0}$ x 100

**[1 mark]**

percentage atom economy = **51.1% (to 3 s.f.)**

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for the correct molar mass of the desired / useful product (2 × 46.0 = 92.0)
> 
> 1 mark for correct substitution with stoichiometric coefficients (`\frac{2 \times 46 . 0}{\left(\right. 2 \times 46 . 0 \left.\right) + \left(\right. 2 \times 44 . 0 \left.\right)}` x 100) **OR** ($\frac{92.0}{180.0}$ x 100)
> 
> 1 mark for a final answer of 51.1% to 3 significant figures.
> 
> **Allow ECF from part (b)** — if the candidate's fermentation equation is wrong, apply the atom-economy method to their own equation and award marks accordingly.
> 
> Allow error carried forward for the final mark from a correct method with a wrong intermediate value.
> 
> Answers not to 3 significant figures or without the % symbol are not accepted.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii) Fermentation is considered a more sustainable method of producing ethanol because:
> 
> Any **two** from (1 mark for each point):
> 
> - Plant crops are renewable / sustainable / can be regrown (whereas crude oil is finite)
> - Growing plants absorb *CO*<sub>2</sub> from the atmosphere, making the fuel (closer to) carbon neutral
> 
> **OR**
> 
> Fermentation is carbon-neutral as there is no net increase in atmospheric CO<sub>2</sub>
> 
> - Fermentation operates at moderate temperatures (30–40 °C) with low energy input
> 
> **[2 marks]**
> 
> "Carbon neutral in principle" is accepted.
> 
> Generic "better for the environment" or "more eco-friendly" without specific reasoning is not accepted.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Remember to include the stoichiometric coefficients in the atom economy expression: (2 × 46.0) on top for two moles of ethanol, and (2 × 46.0) + (2 × 44.0) on the bottom for two moles each of ethanol and CO<sub>2</sub>.
> 
> There is an important subtlety here:
> 
> - Fermentation has only 51 % atom economy (half the mass is "lost" as CO<sub>2</sub>)
> - Hydration of ethene (C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O → C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH) has 100 % atom economy.
> 
> Atom economy alone does not determine sustainability. You should think about the renewable source and the carbon cycle, not just efficiency.

parts.problem_md: Discuss two advantages and two disadvantages of using bioethanol, rather than petrol, as a transport fuel.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Advantages and disadvantages of bioethanol as a transport fuel compared with petrol are:
> 
> Advantages — any **two** from (1 mark for each point):
> 
> - Bioethanol is a **renewable** / sustainable resource
> - Bioethanol combustion produces fewer net emissions of greenhouse gases / lower carbon footprint / is carbon neutral in principle
> - Bioethanol produces **no sulfur dioxide emissions** on combustion
> - Bioethanol can be blended with petrol (e.g. E5, E10) and used in existing petrol engines with minimal modification
> - Bioethanol can be produced domestically from local crops, reducing reliance on crude-oil imports
> 
> **[2 marks]**
> 
> Disadvantages — any **two** from (1 mark for each point):
> 
> - Takes up land that could be used for food production (causing food shortages)
> **OR**
> There is insufficient arable land to meet global transport-fuel demand from bioethanol alone
> - Fermentation and distillation require **energy input** (heating, farm machinery, transport)
> - Bioethanol produces less energy per mole/gram than petrol
> - Destruction of habitats/deforestation to grow crops
> - Crop yields (and therefore bioethanol supply) are **variable**, affected by weather and crop failures, making supply less predictable than crude oil
> 
> **[2 marks]**
> 
> Generic statements ("cleaner", "greener", "better for the environment") without specific reasoning are not accepted.
> 
> The same idea re-stated in different words only gains one mark.

> **[exam-tip]**
> This is a balanced-argument question. You need **two advantages AND two disadvantages** to score full marks. Writing four advantages will cap you at 2 marks.
> 
> It is good practice to pair each point with a brief explanation, not just the assertion because sometimes examiners want a little more. For example:
> 
> - "Renewable because crops re-grow each year" should always earn the mark
> - "It is renewable" alone may not.
> 
> Avoid vague "cleaner" or "greener" without specific reasoning, as these score zero.

parts.problem_md:
A student carries out a small-scale fermentation and wishes to confirm that the organic product is ethanol (rather than ethanal or ethanoic acid, which could form if the fermentation is not strictly anaerobic).

Suggest a simple chemical test the student could perform. State the observation expected if the product is ethanol.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> A suitable chemical test for ethanol with the expected observation:
> 
> 1 mark (M1) for a correct test:
> 
> - Add a carboxylic acid (e.g. ethanoic acid) **AND** a strong acid catalyst (e.g. concentrated sulfuric acid) **AND** warm
> 
> 1 mark (M2) for the matching observation:
> 
> - A fruity / sweet smell is produced (an ester is formed)
> 
> Partial credit — M2 only (the test does not uniquely identify ethanol but the observation is correct):
> 
> - Acidified potassium dichromate(VI), heated under reflux → orange to green colour change (M1 fails as ethanal also reduces dichromate)
> - Phosphorus pentachloride, PCl<sub>5</sub> → white / misty fumes of HCl (M1 fails as ethanoic acid also reacts with PCl<sub>5</sub>)
> 
> Reject (do not score either mark):
> 
> - Infrared spectroscopy (not a chemical test)
> - 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine / Brady's reagent (only rules out ethanal; does not positively identify ethanol)
> - Sodium carbonate / sodium hydrogencarbonate (only rules out ethanoic acid; does not positively identify ethanol)
> - Sodium metal alone (reacts with both ethanol and ethanoic acid; not selective)
> 
> Mismatched test/observation pairs are not accepted.

> **[exam-tip]**
> For "prove this is X" questions, the answer must be a **positive, selective** test for X — not one that merely rules out other possibilities.
> 
> Esterification is the gold-standard chemical test for an alcohol:
> 
> - Only alcohols undergo esterification with a carboxylic acid + acid catalyst
> - The fruity / sweet smell of the ester is unmistakable in the lab
> 
> Common pitfalls flagged in Edexcel mark schemes:
> 
> - Acidified dichromate(VI): turns orange → green for **both** alcohols (ethanol) and aldehydes (ethanal), so it rules out ethanoic acid but not ethanal — earns the observation mark only.
> - PCl<sub>5</sub>: gives white misty fumes of HCl with **both** alcohols and carboxylic acids — earns the observation mark only.
> - 2,4-DNPH only tests for aldehydes/ketones (negative result here) — does not prove ethanol.
> - Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> only tests for carboxylic acids (negative result here) — does not prove ethanol.
> - Infrared spectroscopy is a spectroscopic technique, not a chemical test, so it scores zero on this style of question.

parts.problem_md:
Compound **X** is a chiral aliphatic hydroxy-acid used in pharmaceutical research and as a monomer for biodegradable polyesters. The infrared spectrum of Compound **X** shows the following absorptions:

- A very broad absorption between 2500 and 3300 cm<sup>−1</sup>
- A separate medium-intensity absorption at 3400 cm<sup>−1</sup>
- A strong, sharp absorption at 1720 cm<sup>−1</sup>

Using the Data Booklet, identify the two functional groups present in Compound **X** that give rise to these absorptions.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The two functional groups are:
> 
> - Carboxylic acid  / carboxyl / –COOH **[1 mark]**
> - Alcohol / hydroxyl / –OH **[1 mark]**
> 
> "Aldehyde" or "ketone" is not accepted.

> **[exam-tip]**
> 2-Hydroxybutanoic acid has **two** O–H environments:
> 
> - One from the –COOH group (broad, 2500–3300 cm<sup>−1</sup>)
> - One from the alcohol –OH (narrower, around 3400 cm<sup>−1</sup>).
> 
> Students often miss the alcohol if they stop after identifying the carboxylic acid.
> 
> Two diagnostic rules for distinguishing the two O–H absorptions:
> 
> - Carboxylic acid O–H: very broad, extending down into the C–H region below 3000 cm<sup>−1</sup>.
> - Alcohol O–H: narrower, sitting above 3200 cm<sup>−1</sup> and not overlapping the C–H region.
> 
> A sharp, strong absorption at 1720 cm<sup>−1</sup> confirms a C=O group. The type depends on context:
> 
> - Paired with broad 2500–3300 cm<sup>−1</sup> O–H: carboxylic acid.
> - Paired with C–H absorptions at 2700–2900 cm<sup>−1</sup>: aldehyde.
> - With no accompanying O–H feature: most likely a ketone.
> 
> "Aldehyde" and "ketone" are not supported because there is no C–H absorption at 2700–2900 cm<sup>−1</sup> in the spectrum, and the O–H evidence for a carboxylic acid is clear.

parts.problem_md:
The mass spectrum of Compound **X** shows a molecular ion peak at *m */ *z *= 104.

Elemental analysis of Compound **X** gives the following percentage composition by mass:

- Carbon: 46.2%
- Hydrogen: 7.69%
- Oxygen: 46.2%

Deduce the molecular formula of Compound **X**.
parts.solution_md:
To deduce the molecular formula:

- Calculate the moles of each element in 100 g:

moles = $\frac{\mathrm{percentage} \mathrm{composition}}{A_{r}}$

moles of C = $\frac{46.2}{12.0}$ = 3.85 mol

moles of H = $\frac{7.69}{1.0}$ = 7.69 mol

moles of O = $\frac{46.2}{16.0}$ = 2.89 mol

**[1 mark]**

- Divide by the smallest value (2.89) to find the simplest ratio:

C = $\frac{3.85}{2.89}$ = 1.33

H = $\frac{7.69}{2.89}$ =2.66

O = $\frac{2.89}{2.89}$ = 1

- Scale up to get the simplest whole number ratio:

C = 1.33 x 3 = 4

H = 2.66 x 3 = 8

O = 1 x 3 = 3

- State the empirical formula:

empirical formula = C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O<sub>3</sub>

**[1 mark]**

- Calculate the empirical formula mass:

empirical formula mass = 48 + 8 + 48 = 104

- The empirical formula mass (104) equals the molecular ion peak (*m* / *z* = 104), so the molecular formula equals the empirical formula.

molecular formula = **C**<sub>**4**</sub>**H**<sub>**8**</sub>**O**<sub>**3**</sub>

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct moles per 100 g: C = 3.85, H = 7.69, O = 2.89.
> 
> 1 mark for empirical formula C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O<sub>3</sub>, including the step of multiplying the ratio by 3.
> 
> 1 mark for molecular formula C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O<sub>3</sub>, linked to *m* / *z* = 104.
> 
> Presenting the empirical formula as the final answer without linking to *m* / *z* = 104 is not accepted.
> 
> Allow error carried forward from an incorrect mole step if subsequent method is consistent.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The empirical-to-molecular-formula method has four steps:
> 
> 1. Divide percentage composition by *A*<sub>r</sub> to find moles of each element.
> 2. Divide all mole values by the smallest to get the simplest ratio.
> 3. Multiply by a small integer if the ratio does not give whole numbers.
> 4. Compare the empirical formula mass to the molecular ion peak (*m* / *z*) to find the molecular multiplier.
> 
> Step 3 is the one most students rush. Here the ratio C : H : O = 1.33 : 2.66 : 1.00 is not whole numbers, but multiplying by 3 gives the clean whole-number ratio 4 : 8 : 3.
> 
> Always complete step 4 explicitly. Presenting the empirical formula as the final answer does not satisfy a "deduce the molecular formula" question, even when the empirical and molecular formulae happen to be identical.

parts.problem_md:
The <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum of Compound **X**, recorded in CDCl<sub>3</sub>, shows the following peaks:

| Chemical shift / δ / ppm | Integration | Splitting pattern |
|---|---|---|
| 11.3 | 1 | broad singlet |
| 4.15 | 1 | triplet |
| 3.00 | 1 | broad singlet |
| 1.75 | 2 | multiplet |
| 0.95 | 3 | triplet |

Use the data and the Data Booklet to deduce the structure of Compound **X**.
parts.solution_md:
The structure of Compound **X** is:

![Skeletal formula of 2-hydroxybutanoic acid, with labels showing the 1H NMR peaks for certain protons](assets/011-skeletal-formula-of-2-hydroxybutanoic-acid-with-.png)

**[5 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for identifying the peak at 11.3 (ppm) as the −COOH proton
> 
> 1 mark for identifying the peak at 3.00 (ppm) as the −OH / alcohol proton
> 
> 1 mark for identifying the peak at 0.95 (ppm) as a triplet **AND **that it is a CH<sub>3</sub> group adjacent to a CH<sub>2</sub> group
> 
> 1 mark for identifying the peak at 4.15 (ppm) as a triplet **AND **that it is a CH proton adjacent to a CH<sub>2</sub> group
> 
> 1 mark for the correct final structure of 2-hydroxybutanoic acid
> 
> Skeletal, displayed or structural formulae are accepted

> **[exam-tip]**
> Start every NMR problem by checking the H count. The integrations must sum to the total number of H atoms in the molecular formula. Here 1 + 1 + 1 + 2 + 3 = 8, matching C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O<sub>3</sub>.
> 
> For each peak, ask three questions:
> 
> 1. How many H atoms (integration)?
> 2. What environment (chemical shift)?
> 3. What neighbours (splitting pattern)?
> 
> Useful recognition patterns:
> 
> - Broad singlets above δ 10 ppm are almost always –COOH.
> - Broad singlets around δ 1–5 ppm are usually –OH (alcohol) or –NH, because these exchangeable protons lose coupling to their neighbours.
> - A triplet (3 lines) indicates exactly 2 neighbouring H atoms via the n+1 rule, pointing to a CH or CH<sub>3</sub> next to a CH<sub>2</sub>.
> - The ethyl group signature (–CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>) is distinctive: a 3H triplet around δ 0.9–1.0 paired with a 2H multiplet around δ 1.5–1.8.
> 
> The central CH at C2 couples to **both** the CH<sub>2</sub> (2H) on one side **and** the exchangeable OH on the other. Because the OH proton exchanges rapidly, the CH effectively sees only the CH<sub>2</sub> neighbours and appears as a triplet rather than a more complex multiplet.
> 
> 2-Hydroxybutanoic acid has a chiral centre at C2, bonded to four different groups:
> 
> - CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>– (ethyl)
> - –OH
> - –COOH
> - –H
> 
> A racemic mixture is formed when the compound is synthesised from a planar precursor, so the synthetic product shows no net rotation of plane-polarised light.

parts.problem_md:
2-Hydroxybutanoic acid is synthesised industrially by a two-step route:

**Step 1:** propanal reacts with hydrogen cyanide (in the presence of a trace of KCN) to form 2-hydroxybutanenitrile:

CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CHO + HCN → CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH(OH)CN

**Step 2:** the 2-hydroxybutanenitrile is hydrolysed with dilute acid to give 2-hydroxybutanoic acid.

Draw the mechanism for **Step 1**. Your diagram must clearly show:

- The partial charges (δ+ and δ−) on the C=O bond of propanal
- The lone pair on the cyanide nucleophile
- All curly arrows
- The tetrahedral intermediate and the final organic product
parts.solution_md:
The mechanism for nucleophilic addition of CN<sup>−</sup> to propanal is:

![Chemical reaction diagram showing a cyanide ion attacking a carbonyl carbon, leading to the formation of a hydroxyl and cyanide group on the carbon chain.](assets/012-chemical-reaction-diagram-showing-a-cyanide-ion-.png)

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for the lone pair on C of CN<sup>−</sup> **AND **curly arrow from the lone pair / negative charge to the carbonyl carbon
> 
> 1 mark for the dipole shown on the C=O bond (δ+ on C, δ− on O) **AND **curly arrow from the C=O double bond to the oxygen atom
> 
> 1 mark for the correct structure of the tetrahedral intermediate with a lone pair **AND **negative charge on the oxygen atom
> 
> 1 mark for a curly arrow from the lone pair on the O<sup>−</sup> of the intermediate to the H<sup>+</sup> ion (or H of HCN) **AND **a correct structure for 2-hydroxybutanenitrile, including the OH group
> 
> Accept a one-step mechanism where –OH is formed directly via proton transfer from HCN, provided all arrows are correct.
> 
> Curly arrows must start from lone pairs / negative charge or the centre of bonds.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Two curly-arrow rules that catch students out every time:
> 
> 1. The nucleophile arrow starts from a **lone pair**, not from the atom symbol. Draw the lone pair on CN<sup>−</sup> as two dots, then curl the arrow from those dots to the carbonyl carbon.
> 2. The arrow from C=O goes from the **π bond to the O atom**, not to empty space. The electrons end up on O as a new lone pair, giving the alkoxide intermediate.
> 
> Nucleophilic addition to an aldehyde like propanal produces a **chiral centre** at the former carbonyl carbon. The four different groups bonded to it are:
> 
> - H
> - CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>– (ethyl)
> - –OH
> - –CN
> 
> Attack from either face of the planar C=O is equally likely, so the product is a **racemic mixture** of the two enantiomers of 2-hydroxybutanenitrile. This contrasts with attack on propanone (a symmetric ketone), which does not give a chiral product because the carbonyl carbon has two identical CH<sub>3</sub> groups.
> 
> The chirality of the nitrile intermediate is inherited by 2-hydroxybutanoic acid after hydrolysis, so the synthetic product is also racemic and shows no net rotation of plane-polarised light.

parts.problem_md:
In the industrial process, 8.50 g of 2-hydroxybutanenitrile is hydrolysed with dilute hydrochloric acid:

CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH(OH)CN + 2H<sub>2</sub>O + HCl → CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH(OH)COOH + NH<sub>4</sub>Cl

After work-up, 7.80 g of 2-hydroxybutanoic acid is obtained.

Calculate the percentage yield of 2-hydroxybutanoic acid.

(*M*<sub>r</sub> 2-hydroxybutanenitrile = 85; *M*<sub>r</sub> 2-hydroxybutanoic acid = 104)
parts.solution_md:
To calculate the percentage yield of 2-hydroxybutanoic acid:

- Calculate the moles of 2-hydroxybutanenitrile:

moles = $\frac{\mathrm{mass}}{M_{r}}$

moles of 2-hydroxybutanenitrile = $\frac{8.50}{85}$

moles of 2-hydroxybutanenitrile = 0.100 mol **[1 mark]**

- The molar ratio of 2-hydroxybutanenitrile to 2-hydroxybutanoic acid is 1:1:

theoretical moles of product = 0.100 mol

- Calculate the theoretical mass of 2-hydroxybutanoic acid:

theoretical mass = moles × *M*<sub>r</sub>

theoretical mass of 2-hydroxybutanoic acid = 0.100 × 104

theoretical mass of 2-hydroxybutanoic acid = 10.4 g **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the percentage yield:

percentage yield = $\frac{\mathrm{actual} \mathrm{mass}}{\mathrm{theoretical} \mathrm{mass}}$ × 100

percentage yield = $\frac{7.80}{10.4}$  x100

percentage yield =  **75.0%** **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Answers can be given to 2 or 3 significant figures
> 
> Allow error carried forward from an incorrect mole calculation if subsequent steps are consistent.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Percentage yield calculations follow a fixed three-step method:
> 
> 1. Find the moles of the limiting reagent.
> 2. Use the molar ratio to calculate the theoretical mass of product.
> 3. Divide the actual mass by the theoretical mass and multiply by 100.
> 
> Always check the balanced equation for the molar ratio before calculating. Here the 1:1 ratio of nitrile to acid makes the calculation straightforward. A 1:2 or 2:1 ratio would require halving or doubling the moles.
> 
> A percentage yield above 100% indicates an error upstream, usually in the moles step. Industrial hydrolysis yields of 70–95% are typical, so 75% is a reasonable result here.

parts.problem_md:
2-Hydroxybutanoic acid can undergo condensation polymerisation to form a **biodegradable polyester**. This polyester is being investigated as a sustainable replacement for poly(ethene) in single-use packaging.

Suggest **one** environmental advantage of using this biodegradable polyester rather than poly(ethene) for disposable packaging.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> One environmental advantage of the biodegradable polyester compared with poly(ethene) for disposable packaging is:
> 
> Any **one **from:
> 
> - Polyester is biodegradable so it will not take up space in landfill / will not persist in the environment (unlike polyethene)
> - Does not produce toxic fumes when incinerated
> - Can be manufactured from renewable resources / plant crops (whereas polyethene is from finite crude oil)
> - Forming the polyeter is carbon-neutral in principle / CO<sub>2</sub> absorbed by the plant during growth is re-released on degradation.
> 
> **[1 mark]**
> 
> General statements without a specific mechanism are not accepted.
> 
> Non-environmental advantages are not accepted.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Environmental advantage questions want **specific** reasoning, not vague statements like "it is greener" or "better for the environment." Always tie your answer to one of three concrete angles:
> 
> 1. Biodegradability: which bonds break, and how do microorganisms degrade the polymer?
> 2. Feedstock: is the monomer from a renewable source (plants, fermentation) or a non-renewable one (crude oil)?
> 3. Emissions and degradation products: what does the polymer ultimately become, and is that toxic or harmless?
> 
> Biodegradable polyesters have an advantage over poly(ethene) on all three angles. Pick the most distinct point rather than giving two that overlap (for example, "it degrades" and "it does not persist" are the same point restated).

parts.problem_md:
Aliphatic carboxylic acids can be converted into amides via their acyl chlorides. Propanoyl chloride, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COCl, reacts with methylamine (CH<sub>3</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>).

Write an equation for this reaction and name the organic product.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The equation for this reaction is:
> 
> - CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COCl + 2CH<sub>3</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> → CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CONHCH<sub>3</sub> + CH<sub>3</sub>NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup>Cl<sup>−</sup>
> **OR**
> CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COCl + CH<sub>3</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> → CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CONHCH<sub>3</sub> + HCl **[1 mark]**
> 
> The name of organic product is:
> 
> - *N*-methylpropanamide **[1 mark]**
> 
> "Propanamide" alone and "methylpropanamide" without the *N*- are not accepted.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Acyl chlorides react with amines to form **amides** via nucleophilic acyl substitution. The general pattern is:
> 
> R–COCl + R'NH<sub>2</sub> → R–CO–NHR' + HCl
> 
> A second equivalent of the amine usually neutralises the HCl to form an ammonium salt, as in the equation above.
> 
> When naming amides with a substituent on nitrogen, use the italic ***N*-** locant. The *N*- is non-negotiable: omitting it costs a mark. Write it in italic to show it is a locant, not a position number.
> 
> If the amine had been ammonia instead of methylamine, the product would be **propanamide** (CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CONH<sub>2</sub>), which carries no *N*- prefix because the nitrogen only carries H atoms.

parts.problem_md:
DEET (N,N-diethyl-3-methylbenzamide) is the most widely used insect repellent active ingredient worldwide. Unlike ester-based repellents, which hydrolyse readily in sweat, the amide bond in DEET confers greater resistance to degradation on the skin.

The structure of DEET is shown.

![A skeletal formula of N,N-diethyl-3-methylbenzamide. A central benzene ring is shown. Attached to carbon 1 of the ring is an amide group, consisting of a carbonyl carbon atom double-bonded to an oxygen atom and single-bonded to a nitrogen atom. The nitrogen atom is bonded to two ethyl groups, CH2CH3. Attached to carbon 3 of the benzene ring is a methyl group, CH3.](assets/008-a-skeletal-formula-of-n-n-diethyl-3-methylbenzam.png)

DEET can be synthesised from 3-methylbenzoic acid in a two-step process. A reaction scheme for the synthesis of DEET is shown.

![A chemical reaction flowchart showing a two-step synthesis. On the left is the skeletal formula of 3-methylbenzoic acid, consisting of a benzene ring with a carboxylic acid group, COOH, at carbon 1 and a methyl group, CH3, at carbon 3. A straight arrow labelled 'Step 1' points from this molecule to an empty rectangular box in the middle. From this empty box, a second straight arrow labelled 'Step 2' points to the skeletal formula of DEET on the right.](assets/009-a-chemical-reaction-flowchart-showing-a-two-step.png)

Outline the two-step synthesis of DEET from 3-methylbenzoic acid. For each step, state the reagent(s) and condition(s). Name the intermediate compound formed in Step 1.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> For the synthesis of DEET from 3-methylbenzoic acid:
> 
> Step 1 (3-methylbenzoic acid to acyl chloride):
> 
> Any **one **of the following reagent and condition pairs (1 mark for each point):
> 
> - Reagent 1: Phosphorus(V) chloride / PCl<sub>5</sub>
> - Condition 1: Room temperature / dry / anhydrous
> 
> - Reagent 2: Thionyl chloride / SOCl<sub>2</sub>
> - Condition2: Dry / anhydrous 
> **OR**
> Heat / reflux
> 
> **[2 marks]**
> 
> Step 2 (acyl chloride to DEET):
> 
> - Reagent: diethylamine / (CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>2</sub>NH **[1 mark]**
> - Condition: room temperature
> **OR**
> Heat / reflux **[1 mark]**
> 
> The intermediate is:
> 
> - 3-methylbenzoyl chloride **[1 mark]**
> 
> 3-methylbenzyl chloride (without the 'o' of -oyl) is not accepted as the intermediate name.

> **[exam-tip]**
> For step 1, anhydrous or dry conditions must be specified because acyl chlorides react immediately with water. Any aqueous solvent would hydrolyse the intermediate before Step 2 can occur.
> 
> For Step 2, the nitrogen in DEET has two ethyl groups. This means that the reagent must be a secondary amine, diethylamine ((CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>2</sub>NH). Using ammonia or a primary amine would give a product with the wrong number of substituents on the nitrogen atom.
> 
> The most common naming error is 3-methylbenzyl chloride instead of 3-methylbenzoyl chloride. The intermediate is an acyl chloride, which has a C=O group directly bonded to the chlorine atom (–COCl). A benzyl chloride has a –CH<sub>2</sub>Cl group with no carbonyl. In the name, the suffix -oyl indicates the presence of a carbonyl group.

parts.problem_md: Explain why diethylamine, (CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>2</sub>NH, is a stronger base than ammonia, NH<sub>3</sub>.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Diethylamine is a stronger base than ammonia because its alkyl groups increase electron density on nitrogen:
> 
> - The ethyl / alkyl groups are electron-releasing
> 
> **OR**
> 
> The ethyl / alkyl groups have a positive inductive effect
> 
> **OR**
> 
> The ethyl / alkyl groups push electron density towards the nitrogen atom **[1 mark]**
> 
> - This increases the electron density on the lone pair of nitrogen, making it more available to accept a proton
> 
> **OR**
> 
> This makes the lone pair in diethylamine a better proton acceptor **[1 mark]**
> 
> References to delocalisation into a ring are not accepted. There is no benzene ring bonded to this nitrogen atom.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Do not confuse the basicity of aliphatic and aromatic amines. In diethylamine, alkyl groups donate electrons inductively to N, increasing basicity. In phenylamine, the benzene ring delocalises the lone pair away from N, decreasing basicity. Diethylamine is a stronger base than ammonia; phenylamine is a weaker base than ammonia.

parts.problem_md:
The equation for Step 2 of the synthesis is:

3-methylbenzoyl chloride + diethylamine → DEET + HCl

[*M*<sub>r</sub> values: 3-methylbenzoyl chloride = 154.5; diethylamine = 73.0; DEET = 191.0]

Calculate the percentage atom economy by mass for the formation of DEET in Step 2.
parts.solution_md:
To calculate the percentage atom economy by mass for the formation of DEET in Step 2:

- Write the atom economy expression:

atom economy = $\frac{M_{r}(\text{desired product})}{M_{r}(\text{all reactants})}$ x 100

- Substitute the values:

atom economy = $\frac{191.0}{154.5+73.0}$ x 100 **[1 mark]**

atom economy = **84.0%** **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct substitution of 191.0 as the numerator and (154.5 + 73.0) as the denominator
> 
> 1 mark for correct answer: 84.0%
> 
> Allow error carried forward if an incorrect denominator is used but the method is otherwise correct.
> 
> A correct answer with no working shown scores both marks.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The denominator must include the *M*<sub>r</sub> of all reactants, not just the main reactant. Both 3-methylbenzoyl chloride (*M*<sub>r</sub> = 154.5) and diethylamine (*M*<sub>r</sub> = 73.0) must be summed. The byproduct HCl does not appear in the denominator.

parts.problem_md:
i) State the number of different <sup>1</sup>H NMR environments in a molecule of DEET.

[1]

ii) The N-ethyl groups in DEET give rise to two signals in the <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum. For each signal, state the splitting pattern and explain why that pattern is observed.

[3]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The number of different <sup>1</sup>H NMR enivronments is
> 
> - Seven / 7 **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The two <sup>1</sup>H NMR signals are:
> 
> - A triplet 
> **AND**
> A quartet **[1 mark]**
> 
> Explanation:
> 
> - The methyl / -CH<sub>3</sub> groups each have 2 adjacent H atoms / protons
> **AND**
> By the n + 1 rule, the signal splits into 3 peaks / a triplet **[1 mark]**
> - The methylene / -CH<sub>2</sub>- groups each have 3 adjacent H atoms / protons
> **AND**
> By the n + 1 rule, the signal splits into 4 peaks / a quartet **[1 mark]**
> 
> Allow non-standard terminology for the splitting pattern names (e.g. "3-splits" for triplet)
> 
> Stating just "n + 1 = 4" and "n + 1 = 3" is accepted for the n + 1 rule part of the explanation
> 
> The number of adjacent hydrogen atoms must be explicitly stated to score the reasoning mark, e.g. "Adjacent to CH<sub>3</sub>" without stating 3 hydrogen atoms is not accepted.
> 
> If no other mark is awarded, allow 1 mark for correctly applying the n + 1 rule to either signal.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Students often confuse which N-ethyl signal is the triplet and which is the quartet. Count the H atoms on the **adjacent **carbon, not the carbon bearing the signal.
> 
> - The terminal CH<sub>3</sub> is adjacent to CH<sub>2</sub> (2 H atoms), giving n + 1 = 3: a triplet.
> - The CH<sub>2</sub> is adjacent to CH<sub>3</sub> (3 H atoms), giving n + 1 = 4: a quartet.

parts.problem_md:
The infrared (IR) spectrum of DEET shows a C=O absorption at 1660 cm<sup>-1</sup>.

i) State the typical wavenumber range for a C=O absorption in an amide. Use your Data Booklet.

[1]

ii) Explain why the C=O absorption in DEET occurs at a lower wavenumber than a typical C=O absorption in an aliphatic ketone (≈1715 cm<sup>-1</sup>).

[1]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The typical wavenumber range for a C=O absorption in an amide is:
> 
> - 1630 - 1700 cm<sup>-1</sup> 
> **OR**
> A single value / narrower range within these 1630 - 1700 cm<sup>-1</sup> limits **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The C=O absorption in DEET occurs at a lower wavenumber than a typical C=O absorption in an aliphatic ketone because:
> 
> Any **one **from:
> 
> - The lone pair on the nitrogen atom (partially) delocalises into the carbonyl π-system, weakening the C=O double bond
> - The lone pair on the nitrogen atom reduces the double-bond character of the C=O bond'
> - There is resonance interaction between the N lone pair and C=O group
> 
> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The C=O wavenumber is determined by bond strength. A stronger bond vibrates at a higher frequency.
> 
> In an amide, N donates its lone pair into the C=O, reducing the bond order from 2 towards 1.5 and weakening the bond.
> 
> In an aliphatic ketone, no such donation occurs and the C=O remains a true double bond, absorbing at a higher wavenumber.

parts.problem_md:
A sample of DEET was analysed. The percentage composition by mass was: C = 75.4%, H = 8.9%, N = 7.3%.

The mass spectrum of DEET is shown.

![A mass spectrum. The vertical y-axis is labelled 'Relative intensity' from 0 to 100. The horizontal x-axis is labelled 'm / z' from 0 to 200. Several vertical line peaks of varying heights are visible. The base peak appears at m/z = 119 with a relative intensity of 100%. Other notable peaks appear at approximately m/z = 44, 65, 91, 162, and 191. The peak furthest to the right, labelled M⁺, is at m/z = 191 and represents the molecular ion.
](assets/010-a-mass-spectrum-the-vertical-y-axis-is-labelled-.png)

i) Use the percentage composition data to determine the empirical formula of DEET. Show your working clearly.

[2]

ii) Use the mass spectrum and your empirical formula to deduce the molecular formula of DEET.

[1]
parts.solution_md:
i) To determine the empirical formula of DEET:

- Find the percentage of oxygen by difference:

percentage of oxygen = 100 − 75.4 − 8.9 − 7.3

percentage of oxygen = 8.4% **[1 mark]**

- Divide each percentage by the relative atomic mass:

C: $\frac{75.4}{12.0}$ = 6.28

H: $\frac{8.9}{1.0}$ = 8.9

N: $\frac{7.3}{14.0}$ = 0.521

O: $\frac{8.4}{16.0}$ = 0.525

- Divide all values by the smallest (0.521):

C: $\frac{6.28}{0.521}$ = 12.054

H: $\frac{8.9}{0.521}$ = 17.083

N: $\frac{0.521}{0.521}$ = 1

O: $\frac{0.525}{0.521}$ = 1.008

- The ratio of C : H : N : O is:

12.1 : 17.1 : 1 : 1.01 ≈ 12 : 17 : 1 : 1

- So, the empirical formula is:

**Final answer:** **C**<sub>**12**</sub>**H**<sub>**17**</sub>**NO**

**[1 mark]**

ii) To deduce the molecular formula of DEET:

- Calculate the empirical formula mass:

empirical formula mass = (12 x 12) + 17 + 14 + 16

empirical formula mass = 191

- Compare to the molecular ion:

  - This matches the molecular ion at *m/z* = 191
- So, the molecular formula is:

**C**<sub>**12**</sub>**H**<sub>**17**</sub>**NO** **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> i)
> 
> 1 mark for calculating the percentage by mass of oxygen (8.4%)
> 
> 1 mark for correct empirical formula C<sub>12</sub>H<sub>17</sub>NO
> 
> Allow error carried forward from an incorrect oxygen percentage to the empirical formula, provided the value is positive. A correct empirical formula with no working shown scores 1 mark only.
> 
> ii)
> 
> 1 mark for molecular formula C<sub>12</sub>H<sub>17</sub>NO, with working showing the empirical formula mass equals 191.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The percentages of C, H, and N sum to only 91.6%, not 100%. This tells you another element is present. In this case, oxygen accounts for the difference, and the missing 8.4% must be attributed to it before any mole ratios can be found.
> 
> This is a classic Edexcel trap. A correct empirical formula cannot be reached without first identifying and calculating the oxygen percentage.

parts.problem_md: DEET is more effective than ester-based insect repellents under humid conditions. Explain why the amide bond in DEET is more resistant to hydrolysis than an ester bond.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The amide bond in DEET is more resistant to hydrolysis than an ester bond because:
> 
> - The lone pair on the nitrogen atom delocalises into the C=O bond / the C=N bond has partial double bond character / resonance stabilisation reduces the C=O bond order **[1 mark]**
> - This reduces the electrophilicity of the carbonyl carbon / makes nucleophilic attack by water less favourable / increases the activation energy for hydrolysis **[1 mark]**
> 
> Both marks are awarded for: "The amide C–N bond has partial double bond character (and the C=O is partly weakened); the carbonyl carbon is therefore less electrophilic than in an ester, so harder for water to attack."
> 
> "N is less electronegative than O" is not accepted as the sole explanation.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Both amide N and ester O donate a lone pair into the carbonyl C=O. Nitrogen is less electronegative than oxygen, so it donates more effectively. This makes the amide carbonyl carbon less electrophilic and harder for water to attack. An ester O donates less effectively, leaving the carbonyl carbon more susceptible to nucleophilic attack and hydrolysis.

parts.problem_md:
Direct Air Capture (DAC) is an emerging climate technology for removing carbon dioxide directly from the atmosphere. One promising DAC approach uses a calcium looping cycle, summarised in **Figure 1**.

In a low-temperature carbonator vessel, calcium oxide reacts with atmospheric CO<sub>2</sub> to form solid calcium carbonate. The calcium carbonate is then transferred to a high-temperature calciner, where it is thermally decomposed to regenerate the calcium oxide sorbent and release a concentrated stream of pure CO<sub>2</sub> that can be compressed and stored geologically.

The two stages of the cycle are:

- Carbonator (low T): CaO (s) + CO<sub>2</sub> (g) → CaCO<sub>3</sub> (s)
- Calciner (high T): CaCO<sub>3</sub> (s) → CaO (s) + CO<sub>2</sub> (g)

**Figure 1**

![Process diagram of a calcium looping carbon capture system showing carbonator and calciner units, gas flows, solid CaCO₃/CaO exchange and heat input.](assets/005-process-diagram-of-a-calcium-looping-carbon-capt.png)

Engineers chose calcium carbonate over barium carbonate as the sorbent material in this calcium looping cycle.

Use Group 2 chemistry to explain why CaCO<sub>3</sub> is preferred over BaCO<sub>3</sub> for the calciner step.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> CaCO<sub>3</sub> is preferred over BaCO<sub>3</sub> because:
> 
> - Ca<sup>2+</sup> has a smaller ionic radius / higher charge density than Ba<sup>2+</sup> / ionic radius decreases up Group 2 / charge density increases up Group 2 **[1 mark]**
> 
> Allow reverse argument from Ba<sup>2+</sup> perspective
> 
> "Atomic size" or "atomic radius" is not accepted
> 
> - Ca<sup>2+</sup> polarises the carbonate ion more than Ba<sup>2+</sup> / distorts the carbonate electron cloud more; the C–O bonds in the carbonate ion are weakened more **[1 mark]**
> 
> Allow reverse argument for Ba<sup>2+</sup>: "Ba<sup>2+</sup> polarises less, so the C–O bonds are weakened less"
> 
> "The ionic bond is polarised" is not accepted
> 
> - CaCO<sub>3</sub> requires less heat energy / has a lower decomposition temperature than BaCO<sub>3</sub> / lower running cost / lower fuel consumption in the calciner **[1 mark]**
> 
> Allow reverse argument: "BaCO<sub>3</sub> requires more heat / a higher decomposition temperature"

> **[exam-tip]**
> Examiners note these as the most common mistakes for this type of question:
> 
> 1. Writing "thermal decomposition decreases down the group" without referring to *temperature of decomposition* or *thermal stability*. The change in stability is the key, not the decomposition itself.
> 2. Using "atomic size" instead of *ionic radius*. The Group 2 trend depends on the cation's ionic radius once it has lost its outer electrons.
> 3. Vague answers about "polarisation of the ion" that don't distinguish the polarising cation from the polarised carbonate anion.
> 4. Stating MgCO<sub>3</sub> is more thermally stable than CaCO<sub>3</sub> — it is *less* stable, because Mg<sup>2+</sup> is the most polarising cation in Group 2.

parts.problem_md:
Calculate the standard enthalpy change of reaction, Δ*H*<sub>r</sub><sup>⊖</sup>, in kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>, for the calciner step:

CaCO<sub>3</sub> (s) → CaO (s) + CO<sub>2</sub> (g)

You should draw a Hess cycle as part of your working and use the standard enthalpies of formation in the table.

| Substance | Δ*H*<sub>f</sub><sup>⊖</sup> / kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> |
|---|---|
| CaCO<sub>3</sub> (s) | -1207 |
| CaO (s) | -635 |
| CO<sub>2</sub> (g) | -394 |
parts.solution_md:
To calculate the standard enthalpy change of reaction:

![Hess Law cycle showing thermal decomposition of solid calcium carbonate into solid calcium oxide and carbon dioxide from elemental calcium, carbon and oxygen](assets/006-hess-law-cycle-showing-thermal-decomposition-of-.png)

- Apply Hess's law via a cycle through the elements in their standard states, or use the formation-cycle expression directly:

Δ*H*<sub>r</sub><sup>⊖</sup> = ΣΔ*H*<sub>f</sub><sup>⊖</sup>(products) − ΣΔ*H*<sub>f</sub><sup>⊖</sup>(reactants)

- Substitute the standard enthalpies of formation:

Δ*H*<sub>r</sub><sup>⊖</sup> = [(−635) + (−394)] − (−1207) **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the final answer:

Δ*H*<sub>r</sub><sup>⊖</sup> = **+178 kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for a correctly drawn Hess cycle (CaCO<sub>3</sub> and CaO + CO<sub>2</sub> at the top, elements in their standard states at the bottom, arrows in the correct directions) 
> OR 
> a correct substitution into Δ*H*<sub>r</sub> = Σ(products) − Σ(reactants) with all three signs included
> 
> 1 mark for the final answer of +178 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> (unit required)
> 
> A negative final answer is not accepted
> 
> The positive sign may be omitted only if the working clearly shows an endothermic process

> **[exam-tip]**
> Paper 2 examiner reports described a similar Hess cycle question as "designed to make these marks easy for candidates to achieve but poorly answered". Recurring losses were missing negative signs in the substitution step.
> 
> When drawing a Hess's law cycle you can input the values for the enthalpy changes or add the symbols.
> 
> Always state explicitly whether you are using a *combustion* cycle (Δ*H*<sub>r</sub> = Σreactants − Σproducts) or a *formation* cycle (Δ*H*<sub>r</sub> = Σproducts − Σreactants). These are opposite, and mixing them up is the single most common cause of sign errors.

parts.problem_md:
Direct Air Capture (DAC) using a calcium looping cycle removes CO<sub>2</sub> from the atmosphere by trapping it as CaCO<sub>3</sub> in a low-temperature carbonator and then thermally decomposing the CaCO<sub>3</sub> in a high-temperature calciner to regenerate CaO and release a concentrated CO<sub>2</sub> stream.

An industrial calciner decomposes 50 tonnes of calcium carbonate per hour.

Use your answer to part (b) to calculate the minimum heat input rate, in MW, required to drive this decomposition.

(1 tonne = 1000 kg; *M*<sub>r</sub> (CaCO<sub>3</sub>) = 100.0)
parts.solution_md:
To calculate the minimum heat input rate:

- Calculate the mole flow rate of CaCO<sub>3</sub> per second:

$\text{mass flow} = \frac{50000}{3600} = 13 . 89 \text{kg s}^{-1}$

$\text{mole flow} = \frac{13.89\times1000}{100.0} = 138 . 9 \text{mol s}^{-1}$ **[1 mark]**

- Multiply mole flow by Δ*H*<sub>r</sub><sup>⊖</sup> from part (b) to find the heat rate:

heat rate = 138.9 x 178 = 24720 kJ s<sup>-1</sup> **[1 mark]**

- Convert to MW (1 MW = 1000 kJ s<sup>-1</sup>):

heat rate = **24.7 MW** **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for a correct calculation of moles of CaCO<sub>3</sub> per unit time: 5.00 x 10<sup>5</sup> mol h<sup>-1</sup> or 138.9 mol s<sup>-1</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for a correct energy per unit time: 8.90 x 10<sup>7</sup> kJ h<sup>-1</sup> or 24720 kJ s<sup>-1</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for the final answer in the range 24–25 MW (unit MW required)
> 
> Allow error carried forward from an incorrect Δ*H*<sub>r</sub> in part (b)
> 
> Allow 24700 kJ s<sup>-1</sup> converted to 24.7 MW

> **[exam-tip]**
> Industrial-scale calculations like this lose easy marks on unit conversion. Lay out the chain explicitly:
> 
> - kg s<sup>-1</sup> → mol s<sup>-1</sup> → kJ s<sup>-1</sup> → MW
> - The conversion from kJ s<sup>-1</sup> to MW is a factor of 1000
> 
> A quick sanity check (is 25 MW reasonable for a tonne-scale industrial plant?) catches most slips before they cost marks.

parts.problem_md:
In the calcium looping cycle for Direct Air Capture, calcium carbonate is thermally decomposed in a high-temperature *calciner* to regenerate the calcium oxide sorbent:

CaCO<sub>3</sub> (s) ⇌ CaO (s) + CO<sub>2</sub> (g)

The calciner operates at high temperature. The CO<sub>2</sub> released is continuously piped away to a separate compression and storage facility.

Using Le Chatelier's principle, explain how each of these two operating conditions favours the production of CaO and CO<sub>2</sub> in the calciner.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> High temperature and continuous removal each shift the calciner equilibrium to the right:
> 
> - The forward reaction is endothermic **[1 mark]**
> 
> Allow error carried forward if a candidate uses their own (incorrect) Δ*H* from part (b)
> 
> The answer must explicitly state the direction (forward = endothermic)
> 
> - Higher temperature shifts the equilibrium to the right / to the endothermic side / to the products side / favours the forward reaction, increasing the yield of CaO and CO<sub>2</sub> **[1 mark]**
> 
> Statements giving a direction without justification are not accepted
> 
> - Continuous removal of CO<sub>2</sub> shifts the equilibrium to the right / to the products side; reduces the concentration of CO<sub>2</sub> / reduces *p*(CO<sub>2</sub>), increasing the yield **[1 mark]**
> 
> Self-contradictory answers are not accepted (e.g. "the equilibrium shifts left so the yield of CO<sub>2</sub> increases")

> **[exam-tip]**
> The October 2020 paper 2 report flagged three recurring errors that this question type is designed to test:
> 
> 1. Stating the *direction* of shift but failing to explain *why*. Full marks need both prediction and justification.
> 2. Self-contradictory answers, e.g. stating the equilibrium moves left then concluding the yield of product increases.
> 3. Mixing up the temperature direction, claiming the equilibrium shifts towards the *exothermic* side on heating.
> 
> The fix is a strict two-step structure: state whether the *forward* reaction is endothermic or exothermic, *then* apply Le Chatelier.
> 
> The January 2021 paper 2 report also flagged weaker candidates confusing the rate constant *k* with the equilibrium constant *K*. Temperature changes *K*, but a catalyst does not.

parts.problem_md:
In the calcium looping cycle for Direct Air Capture, calcium oxide and calcium carbonate alternate between two reactor vessels.

Solid calcium carbonate and solid calcium oxide can be distinguished using infrared spectroscopy.

Using the IR data in your data booklet, suggest one absorption band that would be present in the spectrum of CaCO<sub>3</sub> but absent in the spectrum of CaO. Justify your answer.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> CaCO<sub>3</sub> and CaO can be distinguished by their IR spectra:
> 
> - Correctly identifying an absorption with a stated wavenumber range: 1740–1680 cm<sup>-1</sup> (C=O stretch) or 1300–1000 cm<sup>-1</sup> (C-O stretch) **[1 mark]**
> 
> Allow any stated range that falls within the C=O or C-O data booklet values
> 
> - CaCO<sub>3</sub> contains C=O / C-O bonds (in CO<sub>3</sub><sup>2-</sup>) and CaO does not / CaO only contains ionic bonds / O<sup>2-</sup> has no covalent bonds to stretch **[1 mark]**
> 
> "CaCO<sub>3</sub> has more atoms" or "CaCO<sub>3</sub> is more complex" is not accepted

> **[exam-tip]**
> The October 2022 paper 2 (Q22c) report noted that "a significant number of candidates did not state the bonds that produced the peaks but scored the rescue mark for two correct wavenumber ranges". Pair the bond (C=O, or carbonate C-O) with its wavenumber range to bank both marks.
> 
> The January 2022 paper 2 (Q24d) report flagged candidates who "drew the whole molecule, or several atoms, rather than identifying a bond". Answer at the level of the bond, not the molecule.
> 
> For unfamiliar inorganic compounds, treat each ion separately. CaCO<sub>3</sub> is Ca<sup>2+</sup> + CO<sub>3</sub><sup>2-</sup>, and only the carbonate ion has C=O / C-O bonds. CaO is Ca<sup>2+</sup> + O<sup>2-</sup>; the oxide ion has no covalent bond at all.

parts.problem_md:
In the calcium looping cycle for Direct Air Capture, the regeneration step is the calciner reaction:

CaCO<sub>3</sub> (s) → CaO (s) + CO<sub>2</sub> (g)

This reforms the calcium oxide sorbent and releases CO<sub>2</sub> for storage.

Calculate the percentage atom economy by mass for the regeneration of the calcium oxide sorbent.

(M<sub>r</sub> values: CaCO<sub>3</sub> = 100.0, CaO = 56.0, CO<sub>2</sub> = 44.0)
parts.solution_md:
To calculate the percentage atom economy:

- Write the atom economy expression:

percentage atom economy = $\frac{M_{r}(\text{desired product})}{ΣM_{r}(\text{all products})}$ x 100

- Substitute *M*<sub>r</sub>(CaO) = 56.0 and *M*<sub>r</sub>(CO<sub>2</sub>) = 44.0:

percentage atom economy $\frac{56.0}{56.0+44.0}$ **[1 mark]**

percentage atom economy = **56.0%** **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for the correct atom economy expression with *M*<sub>r</sub>(CaO) in the numerator and the sum of *M*<sub>r</sub> of all products in the denominator
> 
> 1 mark for the final answer of 56% (allow 56.0%)
> 
> Allow transferred error if incorrect *M*<sub>r</sub> values are calculated but the expression is correct
> 
> Correct answer with no working shown scores both marks
> 
> 100% is not accepted

> **[exam-tip]**
> Atom economy considers *all* products, even ones you might not normally think of as a "product". For a calcium loop, 56% looks low, but the CO<sub>2</sub> (44%) is itself the captured target, so the cycle is genuinely 100% atom-efficient when both products are useful. Always read the question carefully to see which product is being treated as "desired".

parts.problem_md:
Direct Air Capture using a calcium looping cycle is one approach to large-scale removal of CO<sub>2</sub> from the atmosphere.

Amine-based scrubbing using monoethanolamine (MEA) is an alternative carbon capture technology. MEA absorbs CO<sub>2</sub> from a gas stream at around 40 °C and is regenerated by heating the saturated MEA solution to around 120 °C.

Evaluate the calcium looping process compared with amine-based scrubbing as a method of large-scale CO<sub>2</sub> capture.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Comparing the methods:
> 
> - Calcium looping / decomposing calcium carbonate requires a much higher temperature / much more heat energy (than amine scrubbing) **[1 mark]**
> - Therefore it will have higher energy costs / require burning more fossil fuels (which releases CO<sub>2</sub> and defeats the purpose)
> **OR**
> A catalyst could be developed to lower the temperature for calcium looping **[1 mark]**
> - However, calcium carbonate / limestone is much cheaper / more abundant / less toxic / safer than MEA **[1 mark]**
> 
> Allow reverse argument: MEA is more expensive / more hazardous / produces aqueous waste streams requiring further treatment
> 
> Pure description of one process without comparison earns no marks

> **[exam-tip]**
> Evaluation marks need both sides.
> 
> A common error is to list the advantages of calcium looping only, which is description, not evaluation.
> 
> Use comparative phrasing ("higher than", "cheaper than", "unlike amine scrubbing") and finish with a clear judgement linked to the scale (industrial flue gas vs atmospheric DAC) or the energy economics of the overall capture.

parts.problem_md:
Polyethylene terephthalate (PET) is one of the world's most widely used plastics, with over 70 million tonnes produced annually. The repeat unit of PET is shown in **Figure 1**.

**Figure 1**

![Structural formula of a polyester chain: repeating terephthalate unit with ester links and terminal hydroxyl groups, bracketed with subscript n.](assets/003-structural-formula-of-a-polyester-chain-repeatin.png)

End-of-life PET is increasingly being *chemical recycled* by depolymerising the polymer back to its monomers, which can then be reused to make new PET. One promising approach is *alkaline hydrolysis* of the ester linkages in PET using aqueous sodium hydroxide.

To optimise the conditions for industrial recycling, chemists studied the kinetics of the hydrolysis using bis(2-hydroxyethyl) terephthalate (BHET) — a model PET monomer that contains the same ester linkages as the polymer. The structure of BHET is shown in **Figure 2**.

**Figure 2**

![Structural formula of bis(2-hydroxyethyl) terephthalate, showing a benzene ring with two opposite ester-linked hydroxyethyl side chains.](assets/004-structural-formula-of-bis-2-hydroxyethyl-terepht.png)

The overall alkaline hydrolysis of one BHET molecule is:

BHET + 2 OH<sup>-</sup> → terephthalate<sup>2-</sup> + 2 ethane-1,2-diol

BHET contains the same linkage that is present in PET.

i) Identify the functional group in PET that is hydrolysed by aqueous NaOH.

[1]

ii) State the systematic (IUPAC) names of the two organic products formed when PET is fully hydrolysed in this way.

[1]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The functional group in PET that is hydrolysed by aqueous NaOH is:
> 
> - Ester / -COO- / -CO<sub>2</sub>- linkage **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The systematic (IUPAC) names of the two organic products  are:
> 
> - Ethane-1,2-diol 
> **AND**
> Disodium benzene-1,4-dicarboxylate / disodium terephthalate / sodium benzene-1,4-dicarboxylate / sodium terephthalate **[1 mark]**
> 
> Terephthalic acid is not accepted (reaction is under alkaline conditions)

> **[exam-tip]**
> Under alkaline hydrolysis, the carboxylic acid is deprotonated by NaOH, so you must give the sodium salt (terephthalate) as the product, not the free acid.
> 
> A common slip is to write "terephthalic acid", which is not accepted under alkaline conditions. The diol is unaffected, which means that ethane-1,2-diol is the same product whether the conditions are acidic or alkaline.

parts.problem_md:
Polyethylene terephthalate (PET) is recycled by alkaline hydrolysis. The kinetics were studied using bis(2-hydroxyethyl) terephthalate (BHET) as a model substrate at 80 °C.

The data from three experimental runs are shown below.

| Run | [BHET]<sub>0</sub> / mol dm<sup>-3</sup> | [OH<sup>-</sup>]<sub>0</sub> / mol dm<sup>-3</sup> | Initial rate / mol dm<sup>-3</sup> s<sup>-1</sup> |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0.020 | 0.10 | 8.0 x 10<sup>-6</sup> |
| 2 | 0.020 | 0.20 | 1.6 x 10<sup>-5</sup> |
| 3 | 0.040 | 0.10 | 1.6 x 10<sup>-5</sup> |

i) Determine the order of reaction with respect to BHET, and the order of reaction with respect to OH<sup>-</sup>. Justify your answer using the data.

[2]

ii) Write the overall rate equation for the hydrolysis.

[1]

iii) Calculate the value of the rate constant k at 80 °C, including its units.

[3]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) To determine the orders with respect to BHET and OH<sup>-</sup>:
> 
> - Comparing runs 1 and 2:
> 
>   - [OH<sup>-</sup>] doubles
>   - [BHET] is constant
>   - Rate doubles
>   - The reaction is therefore **first order** with respect to OH<sup>-</sup> **[1 mark]**
> 
> - Comparing runs 1 and 3:
> 
>   - [BHET] doubles
>   - [OH<sup>-</sup>] is constant
>   - Rate doubles
>   - The reaction is therefore **first order** with respect to BHET **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The rate equation is:
> 
> - rate = *k*[BHET][OH<sup>-</sup>] **[1 mark]**
> 
> Allow error carried forward from incorrect orders in part (i)

iii) To calculate the value of the rate constant:

- Rearrange for *k* and substitute values from run 1:

*k* = `fraction numerator rate space over denominator left square bracket BHET right square bracket left square bracket OH to the power of minus right square bracket end fraction`

*k* = `fraction numerator 8.0 cross times 10 to the power of negative 6 end exponent over denominator open square brackets 0.020 close square brackets open square brackets 0.10 close square brackets end fraction` **[1 mark]**

*k* = **4.0 x 10**<sup>**-3**</sup> **[1 mark]**

- Derive the units of *k* from rate / ([BHET][OH<sup>-</sup>]):

units of *k* = `fraction numerator mol space dm to the power of negative 3 end exponent space straight s to the power of negative 1 end exponent over denominator open square brackets mol space dm to the power of negative 3 end exponent close square brackets open square brackets mol space dm to the power of negative 3 end exponent close square brackets space end fraction`

units of *k* = **mol**<sup>**-1**</sup>** dm**<sup>**3**</sup>** s**<sup>**-1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct rearrangement and substitution of values from any run
> 
> 1 mark for the correct value of *k* = 4.0 x 10<sup>-3</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for correct units: mol<sup>-1</sup> dm<sup>3</sup> s<sup>-1</sup>
> 
> A correct answer with correct units but no working shown scores all three marks
> 
> Allow error carried forward from incorrect orders in part (i) or an incorrect rate equation in part (ii)
> 
> Units of "M<sup>-1</sup> s<sup>-1</sup>" or "L mol<sup>-1</sup> s<sup>-1</sup>" are not accepted

> **[exam-tip]**
> When deducing orders from initial-rate data, identify the *one* concentration that changes between any two runs and ignore the rest, then use the rate ratio.
> 
> The most common mistake is to forget that doubling concentration with a 1st-order dependence doubles the rate, but with a 2nd-order dependence quadruples it.
> 
> Examiners want to see the comparison written out, e.g. "comparing runs 1 and 2", not just the order stated as a result with no working.

parts.problem_md:
Polyethylene terephthalate (PET) is recycled by alkaline hydrolysis. The kinetics were studied using bis(2-hydroxyethyl) terephthalate (BHET) as a model substrate.

The kinetics study was repeated at four different temperatures. The values of the rate constant k obtained are shown below.

| Temperature / K | k / mol<sup>-1</sup> dm<sup>3</sup> s<sup>-1</sup> |
|---|---|
| 333 | 1.0 x 10<sup>-3</sup> |
| 343 | 2.0 x 10<sup>-3</sup> |
| 353 | 4.0 x 10<sup>-3</sup> |
| 363 | 8.0 x 10<sup>-3</sup> |

The Arrhenius equation can be expressed as:

$\mathrm{ln} k = - \frac{E_{a}}{R} \times \frac{1}{T} + \text{constant}$

Using any two of these data points, calculate the activation energy E<sub>a</sub> for the alkaline hydrolysis of BHET. Give your answer in kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> and include a sign.

(R = 8.31 J K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>)
parts.solution_md:
To calculate the activation energy E<sub>a</sub> for the alkaline hydrolysis of BHET:

`\ln\left(\frac{k_{2}}{k_{1}}\right) = \frac{E_{a}}{R}\left(\frac{1}{T_{1}} - \frac{1}{T_{2}}\right)`

- Choose two well-separated data points to maximise the temperature range and minimise rounding errors:

*T*<sub>1</sub> = 333 K (*k*<sub>1</sub> = 1.0 x 10<sup>-3</sup>)

*T*<sub>2</sub> = 363 K (*k*<sub>2</sub> = 8.0 x 10<sup>-3</sup>)

- Calculate the natural log of the ratio of rate constants:

ln`open parentheses fraction numerator 8.0 cross times 10 to the power of negative 3 end exponent over denominator 1.0 cross times 10 to the power of negative 3 end exponent end fraction close parentheses` = ln(8.0) = 2.08 **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the temperature term:

$\frac{1}{333}-\frac{1}{363}$ = 3.003 x 10<sup>-3</sup> - 2.755 x 10<sup>-3</sup> = 2.48 x 10<sup>-4</sup> K<sup>-1</sup> **[1 mark]**

- Rearrange the Arrhenius equation for *E*<sub>a</sub> and substitute:

*E*<sub>a</sub> = $\frac{R\times\mathrm{ln}(k_{2}/k_{1})}{(1/T_{1})-(1/T_{2})}$

*E*<sub>a</sub> = $\frac{8.31\times2.08}{2.48\times10^{-4}}$ **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the answer and convert to kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>:

*E*<sub>a</sub> = 69650 J mol<sup>-1</sup>

*E*<sub>a</sub> = **+70 kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for ln(*k*<sub>2</sub>/*k*<sub>1</sub>) calculated correctly using any pair of data points (e.g. ln(2) = 0.693 for adjacent *T*)
> 
> 1 mark for (1/*T*<sub>1</sub> − 1/*T*<sub>2</sub>) calculated correctly using any pair of data points
> 
> 1 mark for correct rearranged expression and substitution
> 
> 1 mark for the final answer in the range +65.0 to +71.0 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> with units; positive sign required for this mark
> 
> Allow error carried forward throughout
> 
> Allow J mol<sup>-1</sup> if explicitly stated (no conversion penalty if value is correct)
> 
> Allow either order (*R* x ln(*k*<sub>1</sub>/*k*<sub>2</sub>) / (1/*T*<sub>2</sub> − 1/*T*<sub>1</sub>)) provided signs are consistent
> 
> A negative final *E*<sub>a</sub> and/or use of °C are not accepted

> **[exam-tip]**
> Examiner reports on Arrhenius questions in paper 4 flag five recurring errors:
> 
> 1. Using °C instead of Kelvin. Temperature must be converted (*T* / K = θ / °C + 273) and the *x*-axis labelled K<sup>-1</sup>.
> 2. Labelling the *y*-axis "*k*" or "rate" instead of *ln k* or *ln(rate)*. Plotting *k* directly does not give a straight line.
> 3. Substituting two raw data points algebraically into the Arrhenius equation rather than using the *gradient* of a line through all the points.
> 4. Freehand lines of best fit instead of using a ruler with two well-separated points on the line.
> 5. Forgetting to convert J mol<sup>-1</sup> to kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> at the end.
> 
> Activation energy is always positive. If your final answer is negative, you have likely forgotten that gradient = −*E*<sub>a</sub>/*R*, so *E*<sub>a</sub> = −(gradient) x *R*.
