parts.problem_md:
Polyethylene terephthalate (PET) is recycled by alkaline hydrolysis. Industrial plants run the hydrolysis at elevated temperature.

Use your value of E<sub>a</sub> from part (c) and the data point at 333 K to estimate the rate constant k at 25 °C (298 K). Comment on the implication of this value for industrial PET recycling.

(R = 8.31 J K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>; k at 333 K is 1.0 x 10<sup>-3</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup> dm<sup>3</sup> s<sup>-1</sup>. If you were unable to calculate a value in (c), assume E<sub>a</sub> = +70.0 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>.)
parts.solution_md:
To estimate *k* at 298 K, apply the two-point Arrhenius equation, taking the data point at 333 K as the reference:

`\ln\left(\frac{k_{298}}{k_{333}}\right) = -\frac{E_{a}}{R}\left(\frac{1}{298} - \frac{1}{333}\right)` **[1 mark]**

- Substitute *E*<sub>a</sub> = 70 000 J mol<sup>-1</sup> and evaluate:

`\ln\left(\frac{k_{298}}{k_{333}}\right) = -\frac{70000}{8.31} \times (3.356 - 3.003) \times 10^{-3}`

`ln open parentheses k subscript 298 over k subscript 333 close parentheses` = -8424 x 3.53 x 10<sup>-4</sup>

`ln open parentheses k subscript 298 over k subscript 333 close parentheses` = -2.97

- Solve for *k*<sub>298</sub> by exponentiating:

*k*<sub>298</sub> = 1.0 x 10<sup>-3</sup> x e<sup>-2.97</sup>

*k*<sub>298</sub> = **5.1 x 10**<sup>**-5**</sup>** mol**<sup>**-1**</sup>** dm**<sup>**3**</sup>** s**<sup>**-1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

The implication of this value for industrial PET recycling is:

- The rate is too slow to be industrially / economically viable at 25 °C
**OR**
The rate would be too slow for a commercial process
**OR**
Elevated temperature is required for an industrial process **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct application of the two-point Arrhenius expression with 298 K and 333 K substituted
> 
> 1 mark for *k*<sub>298</sub> in the range 4–7 x 10<sup>-5</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup> dm<sup>3</sup> s<sup>-1</sup>
> 
> Allow error carried forward from an incorrect *E*<sub>a</sub> value in part (c)
> 
> 1 mark for a comment that the rate / rate constant at 25 °C is too slow to be industrially / economically viable

> **[exam-tip]**
> When extrapolating with Arrhenius, watch the sign convention. ln(*k*<sub>lower T</sub> / *k*<sub>higher T</sub>) is *negative* (the lower-*T* constant is smaller). Setting the equation up as ln(*k*<sub>298</sub>/*k*<sub>333</sub>) gives you a negative answer, confirming *k*<sub>298</sub> < *k*<sub>333</sub>.
> 
> Examiner reports consistently penalise vague "comment" marks here. Link the small *k* value to a real-world consequence: "industrial reactors operate at ~80 °C because residence time at 25 °C would be uneconomically long". Saying only "the reaction is too slow" without any industrial context earns no credit.

parts.problem_md:
Polyethylene terephthalate (PET) is recycled by alkaline hydrolysis according to the overall equation:

PET (s) + n NaOH (aq) → n disodium terephthalate (aq) + n ethane-1,2-diol (l)

i) Predict the sign of Δ*S*<sub>system</sub> for the overall hydrolysis of PET, and justify your prediction.

[1]

ii) Despite a positive total entropy change, the alkaline hydrolysis of PET is impractically slow at room temperature. Explain why.

[2]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The sign of Δ*S*<sub>system</sub> for the overall hydrolysis of PET is:
> 
> - Positive
> **AND**
> A solid giant polymer breaks down into (many) aqueous and liquid molecules (increasing the number of particles / disorder) **[1 mark]**
> 
> "Entropy is positive" is not accepted
> 
> ii) The alkaline hydrolysis of PET is impractically slow at room temperature because:
> 
> - The activation energy for the hydrolysis is (very) high / the reactants are kinetically stable **[1 mark]**
> - Very few particles / collisions have sufficient energy to meet or exceed the activation energy *E*<sub>a</sub> at room temperature **[1 mark]**
> 
> References to *p* (steric factor) or *A* (pre-exponential factor) in the Arrhenius equation are not accepted

> **[exam-tip]**
> This is the thermodynamic vs kinetic distinction clearly stated in the specification.
> 
> One of the most common examples is the Haber reaction at room temperature:
> 
> N<sub>2</sub> + 3H<sub>2</sub> ⇌ 2NH<sub>3</sub> - Δ*S*<sub>total</sub> > 0
> 
> It is thermodynamically feasible but the reaction is kinetically stable because the activation energy for breaking the N≡N triple bond is huge. So, it does not occur at a measurable rate without a catalyst and high temperature.
> 
> Examiners comment on two main errors:
> 
> 1. Saying a reaction "won't happen" because Δ*S*<sub>total</sub> is negative when the question is about kinetic stability.
> 2. Saying a reaction "is feasible, so it will happen quickly".
> 
>   - Feasibility tells you the direction, not the speed.
> 
> For PET hydrolysis, Δ*S*<sub>total</sub> > 0 and Δ*G* < 0, but the high *E*<sub>a</sub> (~70 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> from part c) keeps the reaction kinetically stable until you raise *T* or use an enzyme catalyst.

parts.problem_md:
Polyethylene terephthalate (PET) is recycled by alkaline hydrolysis at ≈80 °C using NaOH. Researchers have also developed *enzymatic* recycling using genetically modified PETase enzymes, which catalyse the same hydrolysis at 30-50 °C.

Evaluate enzymatic recycling compared with alkaline hydrolysis as an industrial method for PET recycling.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Comparing enzymatic recycling with alkaline hydrolysis as an industrial method for PET recycling:
> 
> Any **one **from:
> 
> Advantages:
> 
> - Enzymatic recycling operates at much lower temperature (30–50 °C vs ~80 °C for alkaline) / lower energy cost
> - Enzymatic recycling has a smaller carbon footprint per kg of PET recycled
> - Enzymes are highly specific so the PET does not need as much sorting before recycling
> 
> **[1 mark]**
> 
> Any **one **from:
> 
> Disadvantages
> 
> - Enzymes are sensitive to conditions / may denature
> - Engineered enzymes are expensive to produce / less robust at industrial scale
> - Enzymatic recycling is currently slower per cycle
> 
> **[1 mark]**
> 
> Reverse arguments about alkaline hydrolysis, e.g. uses cheap, abundant NaOH and is easier to scale, but produces large volumes of salt waste, are accepted
> 
> Pure description of one process without comparison earns no marks

> **[exam-tip]**
> For 2-mark "evaluate" questions, give *one point each side*. Don't waste time listing five advantages of one method. Examiners expect a balanced answer with comparative phrasing ("lower than", "unlike alkaline"). A common slip is to write only about advantages of the newer method (enzymatic) and forget that scalability and cost are still on alkaline's side.

parts.problem_md:
Paracetamol (also called acetaminophen) is one of the most widely used analgesic and antipyretic drugs in the world and is on the WHO Model List of Essential Medicines.

Industrial paracetamol synthesis from phenol typically proceeds in three steps — nitration, reduction, and acylation.

![Reaction scheme from phenol to paracetamol via 4‑nitrophenol and 4‑aminophenol, showing reagents conc. H₂SO₄/HNO₃, Sn/HCl and (CH₃CO)₂O.](assets/001-reaction-scheme-from-phenol-to-paracetamol-via-4.png)

The first step is the **nitration** of phenol with a mixture of concentrated HNO<sub>3</sub> and concentrated H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>. The major aromatic products are 2-nitrophenol and 4-nitrophenol; only the 4-isomer is carried forward to the next stage.

i) Give the formula of the electrophile generated when concentrated HNO<sub>3</sub> is mixed with concentrated H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>.

[1]

ii) Explain why phenol undergoes electrophilic substitution with this electrophile more readily than benzene.

[2]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The formula of the electrophile generated when concentrated HNO<sub>3</sub> is mixed with concentrated H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> is:
> 
> - NO<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> / O<sub>2</sub>N<sup>+</sup> **[1 mark]**
> 
> NO<sub>2</sub> without a positive charge is not accepted
> 
> ii) Phenol undergoes electrophilic substitution with this electrophile more readily than benzene because:
> 
> - The lone pair of electrons on the oxygen atom (of the −OH group) delocalises / partially delocalises / interacts with the *π*-system / benzene ring **[1 mark]**
> - This increases the electron density of the ring (making it more susceptible to electrophilic attack)
> **OR**
> This polarises the electrophile more **[1 mark]**
> 
> Answers based purely on -OH being electron-withdrawing are not accepted

> **[exam-tip]**
> For paper 5 electrophilic aromatic substitution, examiners reliably award the activation mark for **lone-pair donation**, not just "electron-donating".
> 
> Always specify which lone pair is delocalised (the O lone pair on -OH; the N lone pair on -NH<sub>2</sub>) and into the π-system of the ring.
> 
> A common slip is to describe -OH as withdrawing by induction (it is, weakly) and then conclude that phenol reacts more slowly than benzene. Lone-pair donation dominates, so phenol is **more** reactive overall. This effect places excess electron density specifically at the 2 and 4 positions, which is why those products dominate over the 3 position product.

parts.problem_md:
The second step in the synthesis is the reduction of 4-nitrophenol to 4-aminophenol using a tin / concentrated hydrochloric acid mixture (Sn / HCl), followed by basification with NaOH (aq).

Write a balanced equation for the reduction of 4-nitrophenol to 4-aminophenol. Use [H] to represent the reducing agent. State symbols are not required.
parts.solution_md:
The balanced equation for the reduction of 4-nitrophenol to 4-aminophenol is:

HOC<sub>6</sub>H<sub>4</sub>NO<sub>2</sub> + 6[H] → HOC<sub>6</sub>H<sub>4</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for the correct organic product (4-aminophenol, HO-C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>4</sub>-NH<sub>2</sub>) **AND **H<sub>2</sub>O as the by-product
> 
> 1 mark for a fully balanced equation: 6 [H] on the left and 2 H<sub>2</sub>O on the right; M2 is dependent on M1 or a near-miss
> 
> Structural, displayed, or skeletal formulae are accepted, provided -NH<sub>2</sub> is shown at the 4 position
> 
> Equivalent equations using H<sub>2</sub> in place of [H] are accepted, e.g.:
> 
> 3H<sub>2</sub> + HOC<sub>6</sub>H<sub>4</sub>NO<sub>2</sub> → HOC<sub>6</sub>H<sub>4</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O
> 
> Equations with the use of Sn are accepted, as long as they are correctly balanced for atoms and charge-explicit equation, e.g.:
> 
> 3Sn + HOC<sub>6</sub>H<sub>4</sub>NO<sub>2</sub> + 6HCl → HOC<sub>6</sub>H<sub>4</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> + 3SnCl<sub>2</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O
> 
> Equations missing H<sub>2</sub>O and/or with -NHO or -NO instead of -NH<sub>2</sub> are not accepted

> **[exam-tip]**
> The conversion -NO<sub>2</sub> → -NH<sub>2</sub> is the standard A-level synthesis route to aromatic amines. Sn / HCl is the common reducing agent.
> 
> Use [H] notation for simplicity unless asked to balance fully with Sn. Each Sn(0) → Sn(II) provides 2 electrons, so 3 Sn supply the 6 electrons needed.
> 
> When balancing organic redox equations using [H], count the change in H on the organic species and add water where necessary to balance oxygen. Here -NO<sub>2</sub> loses 2 O (giving 2 H<sub>2</sub>O) and gains 2 H (on N), so 6 [H] are needed on the left.

parts.problem_md:
The final step is the acylation of 4-aminophenol with ethanoic anhydride, (CH<sub>3</sub>CO)<sub>2</sub>O, to give paracetamol.

i) Write a balanced equation for this reaction, showing the structures of both organic products. You may use condensed structural formulae (e.g. HO-C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>4</sub>-NH<sub>2</sub>) for 4-aminophenol and paracetamol.

[2]

ii) Name the functional group formed in paracetamol that is not present in 4-aminophenol.

[1]
parts.solution_md:
i) The balanced equation is:

HO-C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>4</sub>-NH<sub>2</sub> + (CH<sub>3</sub>CO)<sub>2</sub>O → HO-C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>4</sub>-NH-CO-CH<sub>3</sub> + CH<sub>3</sub>COOH

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for the correct paracetamol structure HO-C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>4</sub>-NH-CO-CH<sub>3</sub> / N-(4-hydroxyphenyl)ethanamide
> 
> 1 mark for a balanced equation including ethanoic acid (CH<sub>3</sub>COOH) as the by-product
> 
> Condensed or skeletal formulae are accepted if the amide linkage and *para*- or 4-substitution are unambiguous
> 
> -NHCO- or -CONH- representations of the amide linkage are accepted
> 
> Structures showing acylation at the phenol -OH (giving an ester) are not accepted
> 
> Equations giving HCl or H<sub>2</sub>O as the by-product do not gain the second mark
> 
> ii) The functional group formed in paracetamol that is not present in 4-aminophenol is:
> 
> - Secondary amide / N-substituted amide **[1 mark]**
> 
> Peptide, ester and amine are not accepted

> **[exam-tip]**
> Ethanoic anhydride is the preferred reagent for industrial acylation because it is less reactive than ethanoyl chloride (so safer to handle) and the by-product (ethanoic acid) is non-corrosive, unlike HCl from acid chlorides.
> 
> When both -OH and -NH<sub>2</sub> are present, the **amine reacts preferentially** because nitrogen is a stronger nucleophile than oxygen. This is why paracetamol synthesis gives the N-acetyl product (an amide) rather than an O-acetyl product (an ester). Confusing the two is a common mistake on paper 5 acylation questions.

parts.problem_md:
A research student carried out the acylation step on a 1.50 g sample of 4-aminophenol with excess ethanoic anhydride, and isolated 1.85 g of paracetamol.

The equation for the reaction is:

HO-C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>4</sub>-NH<sub>2</sub> + (CH<sub>3</sub>CO)<sub>2</sub>O → HO-C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>4</sub>-NH-CO-CH<sub>3</sub> + CH<sub>3</sub>COOH

(*M*<sub>r</sub> values: 4-aminophenol = 109.1; ethanoic anhydride = 102.1; paracetamol = 151.2)

i) Calculate the percentage atom economy for the formation of paracetamol from 4-aminophenol and ethanoic anhydride.

[2]

ii) Calculate the percentage yield of paracetamol obtained from the 1.50 g sample of 4-aminophenol.

[1]
parts.solution_md:
i) To calculate the percentage atom economy for the formation of paracetamol from 4-aminophenol and ethanoic anhydride:

- Write the expression:

percentage atom economy = $\frac{M_{r}(\text{desired product})}{ΣM_{r}(\text{all reactants})}$ x 100

percentage atom economy = $\frac{M_{r}(\text{paracetamol})}{M_{r}(\text{4-aminophenol})+M_{r}(\text{ethanoic anhydride})}$ x 100

- Calculate the answer:

percentage atom economy = $\frac{151.2}{(190.1+102.1)}$x 100 **[1 mark]**

percentage atom economy = **71.6%** **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> A correct answer with no working shown scores both marks

ii) To calculate the percentage yield of paracetamol obtained from the 1.50 g sample of 4-aminophenol:

- Calculate moles of 4-aminophenol:

moles = $\frac{\mathrm{mass}}{M_{r}}$

moles of 4-aminophenol = $\frac{1.50}{190.1}$

moles of 4-aminophenol = 0.01375 mol

- Calculate theoretical mass of paracetamol from 1 : 1 stoichiometry:

mass = moles x *M*<sub>r</sub>

theoretical mass of paracetamol = 0.01375 x 151.2

theoretical mass of paracetamol = 2.079 g

- Calculate the percentage yield:

percentage yield = $\frac{\mathrm{actual} \mathrm{yield}}{\mathrm{theoretical} \mathrm{yield}}$ x 100

percentage yield = $\frac{1.85}{2.079}$ x 100

percentage yield = **89.0%** **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Allow error carried forward from incorrect moles of 4-aminophenol provided the method is correct

> **[exam-tip]**
> The atom economy formula uses the sum of *M*<sub>r</sub> of *all reactants*, not just the limiting reactant. This is the most common slip on paper 5 green-chemistry questions. The numerator is the *M*<sub>r</sub> of the desired product only.
> 
> For % yield, always start from moles of the limiting reactant, then convert to theoretical mass via stoichiometry (1 : 1 here) and the *M*<sub>r</sub> of the product. Examiner reports flag candidates who divide actual mass by starting mass directly as a recurring error.
> 
> Paracetamol synthesis has a high atom economy (~72%) and the only by-product is ethanoic acid (a useful, non-toxic chemical, often recycled), a key reason this route is favoured industrially.

parts.problem_md:
Paracetamol (molecular formula C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>9</sub>NO<sub>2</sub>) is analysed by mass spectrometry as part of routine product purity checks. The electron-impact mass spectrum obtained is shown below.

![Mass spectrum showing relative abundance versus m/z, with small peaks to m/z 80, a major base peak at m/z 109, and molecular ion peak at m/z 151](assets/002-mass-spectrum-showing-relative-abundance-versus-.png)

i) State the m/z value of the molecular ion peak (M<sup>+</sup>) in the mass spectrum of paracetamol.

[1]

ii) The mass spectrum shows a base peak at m/z = 109. Identify the species lost from the molecular ion to give this fragment, and draw the structure of the cation responsible for the m/z = 109 peak.

[2]

iii) Paracetamol (C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>9</sub>NO<sub>2</sub>, accurate mass = 151.0633) and a possible isomeric impurity with formula C<sub>9</sub>H<sub>13</sub>NO (accurate mass = 151.0997) cannot be reliably distinguished using low-resolution mass spectrometry. Explain how high-resolution mass spectrometry can distinguish these two compounds.

[1]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The m/z value of the molecular ion peak (M<sup>+</sup>) in the mass spectrum of paracetamol is:
> 
> - 151 **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The species from the molecular ion is:
> 
> - CH<sub>2</sub>CO / C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>2</sub>O / ketene **[1 mark]**
> 
> The cation responsible for the m/z = 109 peak is:
> 
> - [HO−C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>4</sub>−NH<sub>2</sub>]+ 
> **OR**
> [HO−C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>4</sub>−NH<sub>2</sub>]<sup>+</sup>• **[1 mark]**
> 
> The answer can be drawn, but it must still include the positive charge
> 
> iii) High-resolution mass spectrometry can distinguish these two compounds because:
> 
> - High-resolution mass spectrometry measures *m*/*z* values to 3 or 4 decimal places / to a high degree of accuracy
> **AND**
> The two compounds have different precise / exact masses (due to different combinations of isotopes) **[1 mark]**
> 
> "It can distinguish between fragments with the same nominal mass but different exact mass" is accepted as an alternative to the second part of the marking point
> 
> "High resolution is more accurate" is not accepted on its own

> **[exam-tip]**
> Three common errors to watch for on paper 5 mass spectrum questions:
> 
> 1. **m/z value vs *****M***<sub>**r**</sub>**:**
> 
>   - The mass spectrum reports the *monoisotopic* mass (using <sup>12</sup>C, <sup>1</sup>H, <sup>14</sup>N, <sup>16</sup>O)
>   - For paracetamol this is 151, **not** 151.2.
>   - *M*<sub>r</sub> = 151.2 uses average atomic masses (which include <sup>13</sup>C contribution) and applies to gram-scale calculations only.
> 2. **Loss of 42 vs loss of 43**
> 
>   - Loss of 42 → ketene (CH<sub>2</sub>=C=O, from amide α-cleavage with H-transfer) → m/z = 109.
>   - Loss of 43 → acetyl radical (CH<sub>3</sub>CO•) → m/z = 108.
>   - Paracetamol's base peak at 109 is **loss of 42**.
> 3. **High-resolution MS vs simply higher precision.**
> 
>   - High-resolution measures accurate masses to 4+ decimal places
>   - So, different elemental compositions (e.g. C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>9</sub>NO<sub>2</sub> vs C<sub>9</sub>H<sub>13</sub>NO) with the same nominal mass can be told apart by their accurate masses.
> 
> Always quote the m/z value of the lost species when answering "identify the fragment lost" so the identification is anchored numerically.

parts.problem_md:
The <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum of paracetamol in deuterated dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO-d<sub>6</sub>) shows the following key peaks:

| Chemical shift δ / ppm | Splitting pattern | Relative integration |
|---|---|---|
| 9.65 | broad singlet | 1H |
| 9.18 | broad singlet | 1H |
| 7.36 | doublet | 2H |
| 6.66 | doublet | 2H |
| 1.99 | singlet | 3H |

i) State the total number of unique <sup>1</sup>H environments expected in the spectrum of paracetamol.

[1]

ii) Identify the proton environment responsible for the singlet at δ = 1.99 ppm, and explain why it appears as a singlet.

[2]

iii) Account for the appearance of the peak at δ = 7.36 ppm as a doublet, in terms of the *n* + 1 rule and the structure of paracetamol.

[2]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The total number of unique <sup>1</sup>H environments expected in the spectrum of paracetamol:
> 
> - Five / 5 **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The proton environment responsible for the singlet at δ = 1.99 ppm is:
> 
> - The -CH<sub>3</sub> of the acetyl group / the methyl protons / the CH<sub>3</sub> next to C=O / acetyl methyl **[1 mark]**
> - It is a singlet because there are no protons on the adjacent (carbonyl) carbon atom (so *n*=0, *n*+1=1)
> **OR**
> There are no adjacent hydrogens to couple with **[1 mark]**
> 
> Explanations based solely on the three -CH<sub>3</sub> protons being chemically equivalent are not accepted
> 
> iii) The peak at 7.36 ppm appearing as a doublet is because:
> 
> - The proton(s) on the benzene ring are adjacent to exactly one other proton **[1 mark]**
> - Applying the *n*+1 rule (1+1=2), this splits the signal into a doublet **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Key features of paracetamol's <sup>1</sup>H NMR:
> 
> - **Two doublets** in the aromatic region (6.5–7.5 ppm)
> 
>   - This is the classic 2H + 2H pattern of a 4- or *para*-disubstituted benzene (each ring H couples to its single neighbour on the adjacent carbon)
> - **One singlet** at 2.0 ppm
> 
>   - This is the acetyl -CH<sub>3</sub>, with no -CH neighbours
> - **Two broad singlets** at high δ (>9 ppm)
> 
>   - These are the -OH (phenol) and -NH (amide), both H-bonded and labile (often disappear in D<sub>2</sub>O exchange)
> 
> Three common mistakes on paper 5 NMR questions:
> 
> 1. Confusing **integration** (how many equivalent H at a given environment) with **multiplicity** (how many *neighbouring* H, via *n* + 1).
> 
>   - A doublet always has 2 lines, regardless of whether it integrates for 1H, 2H, or 3H.
> 2. Forgetting that the **carbonyl carbon has no attached H**
> 
>   - So, an acetyl -CH<sub>3</sub> adjacent to C=O always appears as a singlet (*n* = 0).
> 3. Treating the four aromatic H of paracetamol as four separate environments.
> 
>   - *4- or para*-disubstitution gives only **two** aromatic environments (2H each) by ring symmetry, hence the classic two-doublet pattern.
> 
> Always state the *n* value explicitly when applying *n* + 1, and use chemical-shift tables in the data booklet to anchor your assignments.
